title: Logarithmic exponent of integer multiplication
formal:
For a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine \(M\) that exactly multiplies every pair of \(n\)-bit nonnegative binary integers, let \(t_M(n)\) be its worst-case transition count. Determine to absolute error at most \(1/100\) the logarithmic-overhead exponent
\[
\alpha_{\mathrm{mult}}=\inf\left\{a\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}:\exists M\ \exists C>0\ \exists n_0\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \forall n\ge n_0,\quad t_M(n)\le Cn\bigl(\log_2(n+2)\bigr)^a\right\}.
\]
The machine model and quantifiers are specified below. The linear factor \(n\) accounts for the bit scale of the input and output; the requested number describes the power of the logarithmic overhead. The output is the exact product, explicitly written in \(2n\) bits. The exponent lies in \([0,1]\); attaining its infimum is not required.
why: One of the most basic unresolved limits of exact computation, affecting fast arithmetic throughout algorithms.

progress.text: An \(O(n \log  n)\) deterministic multitape upper bound is published. It does not include a matching lower bound.
A conjectured optimal matrix-transposition lower bound is shown to imply the corresponding multiplication lower bound.
New OBDD-width bounds concern a restricted branching-program model and do not close the multitape time gap.

definitions:
For every integer \(n\ge 1\) the input consists of two length-n binary strings encoding integers a,b with \(0\le a,b<2^{n}\); leading zeroes are allowed. The required output is the ordinary binary representation of ab, padded to length 2n. The machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes with one head per tape. Input strings and end markers occupy designated tapes initially, other tapes are blank, and the output must be written explicitly on a designated output tape. In one transition the machine reads and writes at most one cell per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. The cost is the number of transitions, including access, data movement and output. The same machine must halt correctly for every n and every input pair; its tape count and alphabet cannot grow with n. For a fixed correct machine M, let \(t_{M}(n)\) be its maximum running time over the \(2^{2n}\) pairs of n-bit strings. Bounds concern these fixed-machine functions as n tends to infinity. A fresh hardcoded machine for each n is not allowed. No random access, unit-cost arithmetic on arbitrarily long integers, advice, oracle or quantum operations are part of the model. Changing the padded output convention to ordinary unpadded binary changes the cost by only \(O(n)\).

The infimum ranges over logarithmic powers attainable as upper bounds by correct machines in this model. For each candidate exponent \(a\), the machine \(M\), multiplicative constant \(C\) and threshold \(n_0\) may depend on \(a\), but not on the input length or input values. One fixed machine must meet each asserted bound at every sufficiently large length and remain correct at all lengths. It is not permissible to minimize separately over a different hardcoded program for each \(n\).

The explicit output requires \(\Omega(n)\) transitions. The known \(O(n\log n)\) algorithm makes the defining set nonempty and gives \(0\le\alpha_{\mathrm{mult}}\le1\). This definition neither assumes an ordinary growth limit nor requires one machine to attain the infimum. Exponent zero does not by itself assert a linear-time algorithm: it allows separate upper bounds with arbitrarily small positive powers of \(\log n\). Multiplicative constants and iterated-logarithmic factors are not part of the requested numerical accuracy.
answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguously specified real number \(b\) and a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|b-\alpha_{\mathrm{mult}}|\le1/100\), in the stated uniform deterministic multitape model. A certified enclosing interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint; both endpoints must be justified. An exact value also qualifies. Upper bounds must respect the order of quantifiers: each machine is fixed across all input lengths. A lower bound must cover every correct machine in the model. A lower bound on the infimum does not require an attained optimal time or an eventual matching lower bound at every input length. The answer concerns the logarithmic exponent after the linear factor \(n\), not a polynomial exponent of \(n\), a matching full running-time function, or a rounded estimate without a proved error bound.

context_blocks.title: A familiar operation with an unknown limit
context_blocks.text: For example, \(11_2\) multiplied by \(11_2\) is \(1001_2\): the input integers are 3 and 3, and the exact product is 9. The task scales to arbitrarily long binary inputs. The numerical question measures how much logarithmic overhead is necessary beyond the linear cost of handling the input and output bits.

context_blocks.title: Bits and data movement are charged
context_blocks.text: A machine instruction that multiplies two arbitrarily large integers in one step would make the question trivial by placing the entire task inside the instruction set. Here each tape head accesses one cell at a time. Arithmetic on long numbers and rearranging their bits therefore take time. The explicit output alone gives a linear lower bound. It does not establish the additional logarithmic factor in the best known upper bound.

context_blocks.title: What the O(n log n) theorem settles
context_blocks.text: Harvey and van der Hoeven proved an \(O(n\log n)\) algorithm in the multitape Turing model in 2021. This establishes \(\alpha_{\mathrm{mult}}\le1\), but does not determine the optimal exponent. Their 2025 paper records the absence of an unconditional superlinear lower bound in this unrestricted model.

context_blocks.title: The matrix-transposition connection
context_blocks.text: A 2025 theorem relates multiplication to moving data: transposing an \(s\times s\) binary matrix written row by row. Even a \(2\times 2\) matrix with entries a,b,c,d changes its row-order encoding from abcd to acbd. If every multitape machine needs \(\Omega (s^{2} \log  s)\) time for the general transposition task, their theorem implies \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) time for multiplication. The transposition premise is itself unproved, so this is a conditional relationship between lower bounds, not an unconditional proof of multiplication’s optimality.

context_blocks.title: Which later results concern this question
context_blocks.text: Qin’s August 2026 result bounds the width of ordered binary decision diagrams computing a middle product bit on restricted inputs. Width in that model does not bound the running time of every multitape machine. Likewise, arithmetic-operation counts and performance on typical or small inputs answer other questions. This card concerns exact products, the worst input at each length, and one fixed algorithm working at all lengths.

context_blocks.title: What the logarithmic exponent measures
context_blocks.text: The exponent records the power of \(\log n\) multiplying the linear term. For example, a bound \(n(\log n)^{1/2}\) would give \(\alpha_{\mathrm{mult}}\le1/2\). The rates \(n\log n\) and \(n\log n/\log\log n\) both have logarithmic growth exponent one, so distinguishing their iterated-logarithmic factors is outside this target. The infimum convention also avoids assuming that a single optimal machine exists.

sentences: The inputs are two binary integers and the output is their exact product.
Time counts elementary transitions of one fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine.
The requested exponent is the infimum of attainable powers of the logarithmic overhead beyond linear time.
This exponent lies between zero and one and must be determined to absolute accuracy 0.01.
A machine attaining the infimum and matching iterated-logarithmic factors are not required.
